extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and paired with paragraphs from Wikipedia.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and Wikipedia pages.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified using indicator words and length. Questions are kept only if a Wikipedia page is returned in the top five results.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators decide if the question is good, find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, and mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality, reaching 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset has a slight class imbalance, with 'yes' answers being more common.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Question-only models perform very poorly, indicating questions lack sufficient information to predict the answer alone. Factoid questions about simple properties are rare.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing models on their ability to answer naturally occurring yes/no questions and make inferences. The dataset is split into train, dev, and test sets.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine... Each question is paired with a paragraph from Wikipedia that an independent annotator has marked as containing the answer.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine... Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is retumed as one of the first five results

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified: we found selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length, to be effective. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is retumed as one of the first five results

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is good... Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question... Finally, annotators mark whether the question’s answer is “yes” or “no”.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: First, in order to assess annotation quality, three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples. If there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement... On the 110 selected examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: we elected to use singly-annotated examples in the training/dev/test sets in order to be able to gather a larger dataset.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: “Yes” answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set).

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: We also found that question-only models perform very poorly on this task (see Section 5.3), which helps confirm that the questions do not contain sufficient information to predict the answer on their own.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: we test models on their ability to answer naturally occurring yes/no questions... We split these questions into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set
